 PD 3.1: A newer USB PD revision that supports higher power ranges.
 EPR: Extended Power Range, the PD 3.1 mode used for higher-power charging such as 140W.
 PPS: Programmable Power Supply. It allows compatible devices to request changing voltage and current, and is important for some Samsung Galaxy phones and other Android devices.
 QC, AFC, SCP, FCP, and UFCS: Additional charging protocols used by particular manufacturers, devices, or regions.
 Do not choose solely from labels such as “fast charging” or “USB-C.” Check the actual output profiles and, for PPS devices, the stated PPS voltage and current range.

 A “100W charger” often means 100W total, not 100W from every port. The highest-power USB-C port may provide 100W alone, while connecting another device reduces it to 65W, 45W, or another allocation.

 High-output chargers normally become warm or hot under sustained load. Temperature depends on ambient conditions, airflow, enclosure size, input voltage, load, and test duration. There is no single touch-temperature threshold that applies to every model.

 Best GaN Wall Chargers & Charging Stations in 2026
 From a $49 travel-ready GaN brick to a dual-140W 8-port desktop station, here are the five wall chargers and charging stations worth buying in 2026 — and exactly which one fits your setup.
 By Honest Ratings

 How this buying guide was researched:

 In this buying guide
 Every GaN charger listing reads the same way: a big wattage number, a stock photo of a laptop and three phones, and a five-star average that tells you nothing about which port actually gets that wattage. We've now reviewed five chargers and charging stations in depth — from a single 45W travel brick to an 8-port, dual-140W desktop station — and pulled the real, tested differences into one place so you don't have to cross-reference five separate review pages to figure out which one matches your setup.
 This isn't a ranked popularity list. Each pick below earns its spot for a specific reason — desk versatility, laptop-grade single-port speed, international travel coverage, or a genuinely fair budget bundle — and we say plainly where each one falls short.
 Quick Picks
 Best Overall: Moezuti 20-Port 600W Charging Station — the most devices charged at once for the money, with two genuinely fast 65W ports
 Best Budget Pick: Ridge 45W Wall Charger Set — a GaN charger and two braided cables in one $49 bundle
 Best Premium Pick: WOTOBEUS 380W 8-Port GaN Charging Station — two true 140W ports for laptops plus six more outputs
 Best for Travel: URJD 140W Max GaN Universal Travel Adapter — laptop-grade charging plus plug coverage for 200+ countries
 Best for Laptops (Single Port): wegear 140W USB-C Charger — the slimmest true 140W brick in this lineup
 How We Selected These Products
 Every product in this guide has been individually reviewed on this site, with specifications pulled directly from manufacturer listings and cross-checked against verified buyer feedback rather than marketing copy alone. We didn't shortlist by star rating alone — a charger with a shorter review history but a real, verifiable spec advantage (like a true per-port wattage rating) can still earn a spot over a more popular but less capable option. Where a limitation shows up consistently in owner reviews, such as a wattage split under real load, we've carried that into the picks below instead of only repeating the headline number.
 Key Buying Factors
 Shared vs. Per-Port Wattage
 This is the single most misleading spec in this entire category. A charger rated "140W" or "600W" is almost never delivering that number to one device — it's a combined ceiling split across however many ports are active. What actually matters is which ports are engineered to hold a high wattage on their own, and how much the remaining ports drop once you plug in more devices. The Ridge 45W set splits roughly 25W/20W the moment both ports are used; the wegear and WOTOBEUS units both keep one or two dedicated ports at their full rated wattage even with everything else plugged in.
 GaN vs. Traditional Silicon
 All five picks here use gallium nitride (GaN) internals, which is why a 140W brick can be smaller than the 65W charger that shipped with a laptop five years ago. GaN isn't a marketing gimmick — it runs cooler at high wattage, which is also why the higher-output units in this guide add active cooling or thermal-management chips rather than relying on passive heat sinks alone.
 Port Count and Device Mix
 Match port count to how many things you actually charge at once, not to what looks impressive on a box. A single professional with a laptop, a phone, and earbuds doesn't need 20 ports; a household charging four phones, two tablets, and a laptop overnight genuinely benefits from a multiport station instead of a power strip full of separate bricks.
 Included Cables
 Cable inclusion varies more than buyers expect. The Ridge set includes two braided cables and the Moezuti station includes ten short cables covering four connector types; the WOTOBEUS station includes exactly one cable for eight ports, and the wegear charger includes none at all. Factor a $10–15 cable purchase into the real price if the unit you're considering ships without one and you don't already have a spare rated for the wattage you want.
 Travel and Plug Compatibility
 A charger that's excellent at a desk isn't automatically good for travel. If you need built-in international plug coverage rather than a separate plug adapter, that narrows the field significantly — in this lineup, only the URJD adapter is built for that specific job, and even it has confirmed gaps (India, South Africa) worth checking against your itinerary first.
 Safety Certifications
 Look for named certifications (ETL, UL, CE, FCC) rather than a generic "certified safe" claim, plus specifics on what's actually protected against — over-current, over-voltage, overheating, and short-circuit protection are the baseline you want on anything left plugged in and unattended for hours.
 Common Mistakes Buyers Make
 Assuming the headline wattage applies to every port. Read the port-by-port breakdown before buying, especially if you plan to charge a laptop alongside other devices simultaneously.
 Buying a high-wattage charger for a laptop that doesn't need it. A MacBook Air or similar ultrabook is well served by 45–65W; paying for 140W of headroom you'll never use is money spent on capacity that sits idle.
 Overlooking cable requirements. A 140W-rated charger still needs a PD 3.1 / E-Marker-rated cable to hit that speed — a basic cable pulled from a drawer will silently cap the charging rate well below what the brick can deliver.
 Ignoring desk space and portability trade-offs. An 8-port or 20-port station is not something you casually toss in a bag; if you need something portable, a compact single- or dual-port charger is the better starting point.
 Skipping the plug-compatibility fine print on travel adapters. "200+ countries" claims can still have named exceptions — confirm your specific destination before relying on one for an international trip.

Twelve USB-C ports and eight USB-A ports cover phones, tablets, laptops, and legacy accessories at once, and two of those USB-C ports are dedicated 65W outputs that reviewers confirm hold their speed even with the other eighteen ports active. Ten included cables — spanning Type-C, Lightning, USB-C, and Micro USB — mean it works out of the box rather than requiring a drawer full of spare cables.
 Who it's for: Households or shared workspaces charging several devices overnight, and anyone tired of a tangle of individual wall chargers fighting for outlet space.

 At $49, the Ridge set isn't the cheapest charger you can buy, but it's the fairest bundle in this lineup once you account for what's actually included: a genuinely light 85.7g GaN brick plus two braided USB-C cables (1m and 2m) that would otherwise cost $20–30 on their own. The foldable prongs and lifetime warranty claim add up to a set that's easy to recommend to someone who just wants one dependable charger and cables without further shopping.
 Who it's for: Everyday phone, tablet, and MacBook Air charging where 45W shared across two ports is genuinely enough.
 Trade-off: 45W is a shared ceiling, not per-port, and it won't come close to fast-charging a 16-inch MacBook Pro or similar high-draw laptop. See the full Ridge 45W Wall Charger Set review for the port-split details.
 Check the current price on Amazon .
 Best Premium Pick: WOTOBEUS 380W 8-Port GaN Charging Station
 The WOTOBEUS station is the only unit in this guide with two independent, genuinely rated 140W PD3.1 ports — meaning two demanding laptops (or one laptop plus a lot of headroom) can charge at full speed simultaneously, not just in theory but confirmed by owners running sustained rendering workloads without throttling. An active cooling fan and AI temperature-control chip back that up, and six more ports handle everything else plugged into a busy desk.
 Who it's for: Desk setups built around a power-hungry laptop — MacBook Pro, gaming laptop, or similar — that also need to charge several other devices from the same outlet.
 Trade-off: At $99.99 it's the most expensive pick here, it ships with only one cable for eight ports, and reaching the full 140W on a MacBook Pro's MagSafe port needs a separate cable not included in the box. Full details are in the WOTOBEUS 380W 8-Port review .
 Check the current price on Amazon .
 Best for Travel: URJD 140W Max GaN Universal Travel Adapter
 Nothing else in this guide solves the specific problem of needing laptop-grade charging speed and a plug that fits a foreign outlet in one unit. The URJD adapter combines a genuine 140W GaN charger with retractable US, EU, UK, and AU plugs, backed by dual fuses and multi-certification safety hardware, and owners confirm real-world use across a wide range of countries beyond the four built-in plug shapes.
 Who it's for: Frequent international travelers who want to carry one device instead of a separate plug adapter and a separate charger.
 Trade-off: It's noticeably heavier (286g) than a plug-only adapter, it doesn't cover India or South Africa's socket types, and it doesn't convert voltage — dual-voltage devices only. Read the full URJD 140W Max GaN Travel Adapter review before booking around it.
 Check the current price on Amazon .
 Best for Laptops (Single Port): wegear 140W USB-C Charger
 If all you need is one port that genuinely hits 140W in the slimmest possible housing, the wegear charger is the most focused option here — about 27% smaller than standard 140W adapters, with three more ports for a phone, earbuds, or a second device layered on top. Early review data (4.9/5 across 41 ratings) backs up the real-world reliability, at least so far.
 Who it's for: Single-laptop desk or travel setups that want true 140W without the bulk of a multiport charging station.
 Trade-off: No cable is included, the 140W figure applies to one port only and drops fast once other ports are active, and the review sample size is still fairly small. The wegear 140W USB-C Charger review has the full port-output chart.
 Check the current price on Amazon .
 Who Should Buy Which Option?
 Charging four or more devices from one outlet: Moezuti 20-Port 600W Charging Station.
 Want one dependable charger and cables without extra shopping: Ridge 45W Wall Charger Set.
 Need two laptops (or one demanding laptop plus a full desk) at full speed: WOTOBEUS 380W 8-Port GaN Charging Station.
 Traveling internationally and want laptop-grade charging in the same unit as your plug adapter: URJD 140W Max GaN Travel Adapter.
 One laptop, minimal bulk, true 140W on a single port: wegear 140W USB-C Charger.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Do I need a 140W charger if I only own a phone and a tablet?
 No. A phone and tablet combined rarely draw more than 45–65W total, so a 140W charger is unused capacity in that scenario. Save the money and put it toward a charger in the 45–65W range instead.
 Will a multiport charging station slow down my laptop's charging speed?
 It depends on the unit. Stations with a dedicated high-wattage port, like the Moezuti's two 65W ports or the WOTOBEUS's two 140W ports, are built to hold laptop-charging speed even with other devices connected. Cheaper multiport chargers without a dedicated high-wattage port will split power evenly and can meaningfully slow a laptop down.
 Do GaN chargers actually charge faster than older silicon chargers?
 GaN itself doesn't change the charging protocol or speed directly — a device still only draws what it's designed to accept. What GaN changes is size and heat: the same wattage fits in a smaller, cooler-running case, which is why high-wattage chargers today are practical to carry rather than the brick-sized units from silicon-based designs years ago.
 Is it safe to leave a multiport charging station plugged in overnight?
 The units in this guide include named safety certifications and protections — over-current, over-voltage, overheating, and short-circuit safeguards — and reviewers for both the Moezuti and WOTOBEUS stations specifically report using them for overnight charging without issues. As with any electronics left plugged in unattended, buy from a listing with real certification claims rather than a generic "safe" statement.
 Can I use a US-market GaN charger abroad?
 Only if it accepts 100–240V input (most modern GaN chargers do) and you have a plug adapter for the local outlet shape. A plug adapter alone doesn't add fast-charging capability if the charger itself isn't already dual-voltage — check the input voltage rating on the specific model before traveling.
 What's the difference between a "shared" wattage rating and a "per-port" rating?
 A shared rating is the maximum the entire unit can output across all ports combined; a per-port rating is what a single specific port can deliver on its own. Nearly every multiport charger uses shared ratings for most of its ports, reserving one or two dedicated ports (if any) for a guaranteed high-wattage number.
 Final Recommendation
 For most people replacing a drawer full of mismatched chargers, the Moezuti 20-Port 600W Charging Station is the easiest recommendation — it covers the widest range of devices for the lowest price per port in this guide. If your setup revolves around a single demanding laptop that needs guaranteed full-speed charging alongside several other devices, the WOTOBEUS 380W 8-Port GaN Charging Station is worth the higher price. And if you're buying for travel specifically, skip straight to the URJD 140W Max GaN Travel Adapter rather than trying to make a desk-focused charger work abroad.

How a 300W USB-C Desktop Charger Can Replace Multiple Power Adapters？

How a 300W USB-C Desktop Charger Can Replace Multiple Power Adapters？
05/10/2026

Most desks have the same problem: a drawer of mismatched chargers, two or three power bricks trailing across the desk, and never a free wall socket when you need one.

If your laptop, phone and tablet all charge over USB-C, most of that can go.

A single USB-C desktop charger can negotiate a supported power level with each compatible device, within the charger’s available power budget, so one unit can charge several devices from one socket.

At 300W total output, it provides substantial headroom for several demanding devices, although the power available to each device still depends on the active port combination.

Here’s how a USB-C desktop charger replaces multiple adapters, what a 300W model can power at the same time, and what to look for before you buy.

Key Takeaways
USB-C Power Delivery negotiates a supported power level between the charger and each compatible device, allowing one charger to serve phones, tablets and laptops.
GaN supports high power density, helping high-wattage chargers fit into more compact form factors.
A 300W multi-port charger can support several demanding devices at once, but the power available to each device depends on the active port combination and power-allocation rules.
Total power is shared across the ports, so connecting more devices can change the wattage available to each port.
Match both the total output and per-port capability to your devices, and check the applicable conformity requirements and built-in protection features.
What is a USB-C desktop charger, and why can one replace several adapters?

A USB-C desktop charger is a mains-powered charging station with several USB-C ports and a high total wattage. It can replace multiple adapters because USB-C Power Delivery allows compatible chargers and devices to negotiate an appropriate supported power level.

The reason it works is a standard called USB-C Power Delivery.

The charger and device communicate to agree on a supported voltage and current before higher power is delivered. That allows the same charger to supply low-power accessories and more demanding laptops, provided the charger, device and cable support the required profile.

As Tom’s Hardware notes, the same USB-C charging ecosystem can serve devices with very different power requirements because each compatible device negotiates the level it supports.

A desktop model sits within the broader category of USB-C chargers, but adds more ports and a higher shared power budget for a fixed desk setup.

If you also need something portable, our guide explains how single-port and multi-port chargers compare for travel.

How 300W and GaN let one charger do it all

Two things make a one-charger desk possible: USB-C Power Delivery now supports much higher power levels, and GaN technology enables high power density in a more compact charger design.

USB Power Delivery originally operated at lower maximum power levels, while USB PD 3.1 Extended Power Range can now support up to 240W over USB-C with compatible hardware. Reaching the higher EPR power levels also requires suitably rated cables and compatible devices.

A 300W desktop charger uses its total output budget across several ports. The 300W figure refers to the charger’s combined output capacity, not the output of a single USB-C port.

The other half is the power-conversion technology inside.

Chargers built with GaN, or gallium nitride, can switch efficiently at high frequencies and support higher power density than conventional designs, helping high-output chargers use a more compact form factor.

That makes it possible to combine substantial total output and multiple ports in a desktop-sized unit rather than relying on several separate adapters.

One thing to understand is how the power is shared. The total wattage is distributed across the active ports and can be reallocated as devices are connected or disconnected. A higher total output gives the charger more headroom, but it does not mean every port can deliver its individual maximum at the same time.

What a 300W, 8-port charger can power at once

A 300W charger provides substantial total capacity for a multi-device desk, but actual charging performance depends on the devices connected, the ports being used, the charger’s allocation rules and the cables involved.

Here are some current examples of charging requirements for common devices:

Device	Example charging requirement
iPhone 17 / 17 Pro / 17 Pro Max	40W or higher USB-C adapter for Apple’s current fast-charge test of around 50% in 20 minutes
iPad Pro (M5)	60W or higher USB-C adapter for fast charging to around 50% in 30 minutes
MacBook Air	Around 30W to 35W for standard charging on many models; 67W or 70W for fast charging on supported models
14-inch MacBook Pro	Adapter requirements vary by model; supported fast-charge configurations commonly use 96W or higher
16-inch MacBook Pro	140W for supported fast charging
Windows laptop	Varies by model; check the manufacturer’s USB-C Power Delivery input specification
Mirrorless camera	Varies by model; check whether the camera supports USB-C charging or USB Power Delivery and its stated input requirement

For a model-by-model Apple laptop breakdown, see our guide to how many watts your MacBook charger needs.

Add a realistic desk together and the benefit of a high total power budget becomes clearer.

A videographer might connect a 16-inch MacBook Pro, an iPad Pro, an iPhone, a camera and earbuds at the same time. Their combined requirements can fit within a 300W total budget, but the actual power delivered to each device still depends on the active port combination, each device’s negotiated charging profile and the USB-C to USB-C cables being used.

The caveat is that per-port wattage matters just as much as the total. A 16-inch MacBook Pro can use a 140W-capable connection for supported fast charging, but on the Nexode Pro 300W, USB-C1, USB-C2 and USB-C3 each support up to 140W when used individually. Once several devices are connected, the available output follows the relevant multi-port power distribution.

That is why both the total power budget and the per-port allocation matter when you build a multi-device setup.

The UGREEN Nexode Pro Smart Display Desktop Charger (300W, 8-Port, GaN, 5 Charging Modes) is designed for multi-device desk setups, with a 300W total shared output and USB-C1, USB-C2 and USB-C3 each supporting up to 140W when used individually.

The built-in smart display gives users a clearer view of how connected devices are charging.

Who benefits most from a 300W desktop charger?

Anyone with a multi-device desk can benefit, but the format is most useful for people who regularly charge several higher-power devices at the same time.

If you are still deciding between a fixed desktop format and something more portable, our comparison explains whether a wall charger or desktop charger fits your setup.

Photographers and videographers may need to recharge a laptop, camera equipment, a phone and a tablet between shoots, making a high-capacity multi-port charger useful at a fixed workstation.
Content creators often use a laptop, phone, recorder, light and earbuds, allowing one desktop unit to reduce the number of separate adapters on the desk.

What to look for in a USB-C desktop charger

Judge a desktop charger on total wattage, per-port wattage, the number and mix of ports, power density and applicable conformity requirements, rather than the headline wattage alone.

Start with total wattage: add up the devices you expect to charge at the same time and leave some headroom, since the available power is shared. Then check the multi-port allocation table and per-port limits, because a demanding laptop needs a port combination that can provide the power it requires.

Count the ports you need and favour USB-C for modern compatible devices. GaN can help support higher power density and a more compact design, while a display or app can be useful if you want to monitor and manage charging.

Finally, consider compliance and built-in protection features. Thermal protection also matters, and our guide explains when charger heat is normal and when you should investigate it.

For electrical equipment placed on the market in Great Britain, either UKCA or CE marking can currently be used where the applicable conformity requirements are met. Northern Ireland follows separate product-marking rules. Treat conformity marking as one part of the compliance picture alongside manufacturer information, appropriate electrical protections and correct use.

The wrap-up

A 300W USB-C desktop charger can reduce the number of separate adapters on a multi-device desk. USB Power Delivery allows compatible devices to negotiate supported charging levels, while GaN technology enables high power density in a compact desktop format.

The important numbers are both the total output and the power available through the specific ports you use. Check those figures, the cable requirements and the applicable conformity information before choosing a charger.

The UGREEN Nexode Pro Smart Display Desktop Charger (300W, 8-Port, GaN, 5 Charging Modes) is one example built around that approach, combining a 300W shared power budget, multiple ports, charging-status information and configurable power allocation in one desktop unit.

What is a USB-C desktop charger?
A mains-powered charging station with several USB-C ports and a high total wattage. With USB Power Delivery, compatible chargers and devices can negotiate supported power levels, allowing one unit to charge a wide range of devices from smaller accessories to laptops.
Can one charger replace all my adapters?
For many compatible USB-C devices, it can replace several separate adapters. The charger still needs the right total output, port capabilities and supported charging profiles for the devices you connect.
How many devices can a 300W charger power at once?
A 300W model can support many multi-device desk setups, but the number of devices that can charge at their preferred power levels depends on the active ports, each device’s requirements and the charger’s power-allocation rules.

Does adding more devices slow the charging?
It can change the power available to individual ports because the charger’s total output is shared. A 300W total budget provides more headroom for multiple devices, but the final allocation still depends on the active port combination and each device’s negotiated demand.
Is a high-wattage charger safe?
A compliant charger should incorporate appropriate power and thermal protections and meet the applicable conformity requirements for the market where it is sold. Follow the manufacturer’s specifications and use compatible cables and devices.

Powerful fast charging hub with DC port: Ugreen Nexode Pro 300W Desktop Charger review - Notebookcheck Review 
 Verdict – Plenty of power and smart features, but not quite the perfect one-charger solution
 With six USB-C ports, one USB-A, and one 240W DC port, the Ugreen Nexode Pro 300W Desktop Charger stands as a powerful charging hub that can power all devices kept on a desk. The built-in display has smart features, and the app support with WiFi controls is a nice bonus. 
 It's pretty efficient as well, and doesn't get too hot during prolonged high-power output sessions. The display also shows accurate power readings, and the overall design is quite sleek. 
 However, Ugreen doesn't include a DC cable with the desktop charger, and the package lacks laptop charging adapters. The limited port availability of the DC Turbo Charging mode, especially in the 20V setting, is another aspect that potential buyers should consider.
 Pros
 + Up to 140W from three USB-C ports 
 + Can power up to seven devices simultaneously 
 + Accurate real-time power readings 
 + Proper app support with controls over WiFi 
 + Customizable port power controls 
 + Efficient with minimal heat buildup 
 Cons
 - DC cable not included 
 - Laptop charging adapters not included 
 - 20V DC mode disables the other ports 
 4
 Price and availability
 The Ugreen Nexode Pro 300W Desktop Charger launched with a regular retail price tag of $199.99. It's available on the official store and on Amazon .

 4
 Ugreen released the Nexode Pro 300W Desktop Charger as a direct competitor to the Cuktech 30 Ultra Charging Station that we recently reviewed. Like Cuktech's model, there's a DC port, which allows it to stand as a replacement for the laptop charger, but there are some aspects where Ugreen's charging solution lags behind, and there's a potential deal-breaking aspect for some of the targeted customers.

 300W

 Package contents 
 1x AC cable, 1x base, 1x user manual, and 1x desktop charger 
 The package content is minimal, and that's a problem
 Ugreen doesn't include much in the package of the Nexode Pro 300W Desktop Charger. In the box, there's the charger itself, a stand, a user manual, and a power cable. While this set of included items is fine for the average user, the lack of a cable for the DC port and laptop charging adapters is a problem.
 Package contents 
 For instance, the competing Cuktech 30 Ultra comes with a high-quality DC male-to-male cable, and as we noted in our review, the package also includes adapters for laptops from Lenovo, HP, Dell, Acer, Asus ROG, Razer, and MSI. 
 In the case of the desktop charger from Ugreen, two separate purchases are required to charge laptops through the DC port. One of them is a male-to-male 5525 cable, and the second one is the right charging adapter for the laptop. Among the two, the latter can be a bit challenging to acquire in some regions.
 Ugreen Nexode Pro 300W Desktop Charger looks sleek, and it has a multifunction screen
 Moving beyond the packaging, the desktop charger itself has a sleek overall outlook, and it should blend perfectly on top of desks. The included stand is adjustable, offering a one-step height adjustment, and the buttons on the top allow easy management of the charging modes and other settings.
 The included stand 
 The desktop charger with the stand 
 There's a smart display on the front that shows all the important charging information at a glance, including the power output of each port. Ugreen has also integrated a nifty standby mode that shows the clock, day, and date, and it also allows users to upload custom wallpapers.
 The standby mode 
 Power output readings from each port 
 This desktop charger has eight ports and can power seven devices simultaneously
 There are a total of eight ports, and among them, six are USB Type-C ports. As Ugreen highlights, the first three USB-C ports can deliver up to 140W, and the test results from the Fnirsi FNB58 USB tester confirm this. These three support PD3.1 , making them ideal for powering laptops with USB-C charging support.
 USB-C1 test snapshot 
 USB-C2 test snapshot 
 USB-C3 test snapshot 
 As for the other Type-C ports, the USB-C4 and USB-C5 have support for 100W fast charging, and they bring PD3.0 compatibility. These are good recharging for tablets, power banks, and gaming handhelds . The last USB-C port, the USB-C6, maxes out at 30W, but it also supports PD3.0. It's worth noting that all the USB-C ports have support for other protocols other than PD, including AFC and QC4.0 .

 There's a USB-A port on the side, which can deliver up to 22.5W, and with this, the desktop charger gains the ability to power seven devices at the same time. Regarding the DC port, when it's turned on, only the USB-C1, C2, and C3 work at the 12V and 15V modes. When the 20V mode is selected, all the other ports stop working, and it's worth noting that the DC port maxes out at 240W .

 The charger is quite efficient, and it shows accurate power output readings
 To put the efficiency of the desktop charger to the test, we compared the power intake from the wall with the power output. As shown in the pictures attached below, there's around a 10W difference, which remains the same in multiple instances. It's worth noting that this comparison was made with the built-in display turned on, but its brightness was set to 20%.

 The power output readings from the built-in display are pretty accurate as well. We tested it with the Fnirsi FNB58 USB tester, and as shown in the pictures below, the charger can show values in real time, and they can be about 1W off.
 Power output reading accuracy test 
 Ugreen Nexode Pro 300W Desktop Charger has advanced app support with over-the-WiFi controls
 One nifty feature of the desktop charger is that it has advanced app support. It's possible to get it paired in WiFi and Bluetooth modes. The former allows users to monitor the charging status remotely, without being near the device. With the WiFi connection , the custom charging mode unlocks, and this can be quite handy for specific scenarios. 
 Through the app, users can set custom power values to each of the ports, and it's even possible to turn the ports off by setting the value to 0. That means users can remotely turn devices on and off.
